utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later two of those nine have been found to be dead. And today I should think that even more have been found to be dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- it doesn't -- this doesn't relate to the question -- my original question. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the -- on a similar topic, you started your answers there with the -- the fact that the ICRC list is -- is based upon mainly family members or close friends that are reporting their -- their loved ones or neighbours missing. Did you take into account that there may be missing people that had no family members left to report them? And, if so, did you get any feel in your work for how many people there might be in that category, if any?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's an issue we have been concerned about all the time, and the indication of this as a case is that the number of reported missing persons is -- has increased by low numbers. It increased from 2000 to 2005. The table on the screen shows that it increased by at least 29. So it's a low number. Another indication that there are some people in that category that were dead but not reported as missing is that -- in the exhumations there are some people who are found and identified with a unique profile who are not -- doesn't match with any -- the name of the person is not found. A few hundred. So that indicates that there was nobody who -- to report them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that based on the -- your knowledge that ICMP took blood from many of the relatives reporting their people missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that if a named person shows up in a mass grave --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. It's not named them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about a named person? Are there named people that don't connect to any of the missing lists that -- that you recall?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Then we wouldn't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because only if he was wearing a name tag would we know the name. But to give you a couple of examples that may illuminate this is that, say, a man - in most -- most of the missing are men - was newly married, he had no children, his parents are not alive, then reported by his wife as missing, but he would have no common -- or very little common DNA material compared to his wife since then he would not -- could not be found as identified as the husband of somebody. He can be then identified as a son or father or cousin but not as a husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're speaking of individuals identified in mass graves by name because of a blood DNA connection?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And people that are identified as unique individuals through DNA but --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But no name; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true. Now there are some cases especially at the beginning of this process that people found in graves and were identified without DNA analysis because -- before this became common. There were 68 such persons who on our missing lists -- first missing list who were identified as dead. I don't know the exact way this was done, but this could be through a unique features, clothing, dental features, which was the way identification was done previously before DNA analysis become the very reliable and common source of identifying people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. It's -- let's take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. We take a break of 20 minute, Mr. Brunborg. We'd like to see you back after that. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you made an oral request to sit -- oh, Mr. Lukic is not there. I apologise. Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Lukic made a request to sit less than five days and to adapt the schedule. Now, in view of the upcoming recess which may change circumstances considerably where it gives three weeks to have rest, the Chamber will not decide on the request now. It invites the Defence to consider the effect of three weeks of non-sitting and expresses that the preferred way of further pursuing the issue would be in a well-motivated written motion with adequate supporting materials. Now that is the request of this morning, which addresses the present situation. Of course, the other matter, separate matter, although not entirely without a link but a separate issue, is the pending request for a certificate for an appeal. The Chamber has not received any response to the request for a certificate yet, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. McCloskey. When could we expect that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll look into that. I don't have that right now, Mr. President. I'm sure there's been a -- close to a decision made but I'll see where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Chamber would -- may have some preference in receiving that expeditiously so that when we have the recess that we do not lose unnecessary time deciding on the matter, whatever direction that decision may go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I don't see any reason it should take very long. So I will look into that and get back to you and -- and just -- on a related subject, just so you know, I think we've seen -- we're hoping we're going to be finished with the Prosecution's case by October, maybe going into November if, you know, things happen but that's what we're looking at. We have first the Srebrenica component, Mr. Butler and Mr. Janc, the significant witnesses shortly after we get back and then some other expert witnesses for the rest of the case. But we're hoping to end, end of October, perhaps early November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No results yet for coffee or tea meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, I can report that the videos D246 MFI and D245 MFI have been copied and given to the Prosecution as -- earlier than the seven days that had been anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may continue your examination .

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, while we have this -- this chart up here, we can all see that you've got a very exact total of number of missing, 7.692 at the time of this report several years ago. Can you tell us is this meant to be an exact figure? Is it less? Is it more? Is it -- how should we take this figure? Is it conservative? Is it liberal? What is it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In our work we were also -- we were always trying to be conservative. So if there was any doubt about person whether he or she was missing or -- or dead or alive, we -- or did not much up with something we deleted the person. So it should be considered a conservative estimate. And this has been strengthened by other time since more persons have been added to the missing list, mostly because they have been found to be dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'll get into that briefly as -- as the final chapter, the DNA IDs and how that fit in your report. But before we get there, could we go to your actual list itself. It should be 65 ter 11270. And this is the first page of the list you created; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 8 in e-court. This is mostly a list of names, Mr. President, so it has not been translated, but if we can just blow up the one on the right side. And we can -- we can see here that the -- yes, right there is fine, that the name, the full names on the left are the name, last first, first, father's, the next is sex, the next date of birth, the next date and place of disappearance, then status, then registration number, and then a code and a grave-site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is that a public document? Can this list be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Out of an abundance of caution we should not broad it. There is still a possibility that there are people on this list that have -- family has not been notified and thank you for that reminder. I hope, in consultation with ICMP, we will be able to make this list public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I don't want to go over all this. I think it speaks for itself but is this very closely modelled after the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. With one very important addition and that is the identified, which means dead. I think in all the identified cases the information comes from ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So this is a very important change from previous editions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me -- I'll go to a table now. Unless there's any questions on the list in particular. We -- we see familiar sounding names for place of disappearance and the dates of disappearance. This is all the information from the family members that reported this to ICRC or PHR?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They could be information from other sources as well through the merging of different lists. The ICMP has their own missing list, and also, in some case, we took information from the 1991 census, especially on date of birth. If it was incomplete on the ICRC list and we were convinced that it was a true match with 1991 census, we could then transfer the full date of birth from the 1991 census to our -- the -- our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I think that is explained in your report. If we could now go to 65 ter 25879. And before we get there, can you tell us, as the -- as you've noted, the Chamber has heard evidence of very large numbers of people identified by name either from areas that have been noted by the Prosecution as mass graves or areas that have been noted on the surface in the area. Having those DNA-identified names in the thousands, does that help you in any way as a quality control or a double-check of the -- of the accuracy of -- of your -- of your list, which we know is fundamentally based on relatives reporting loved ones.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Definitely. We started out with looking at lists -- or missing persons. We were not sure whether -- we did not know whether they were dead or not or even survivors or not. The hypothesis was that they had been killed after the fall of Srebrenica but we did not know for sure. Excuse me, my voice needs to be cleared. But the findings of ICMP since 2001 strongly supports the original list of missing persons. Actually, these lists corroborate each other, and since they come from independent sources they strongly support each other. They are highly consistent. They could not -- one of these lists could not be wrong all -- their own because then the other lists would -- would find that, that this was wrong. So they're completely supportive of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say -- sorry. You say the other list would say find that, that was wrong. How --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I was to the clear. Say, if there was one of these lists was strongly biased or full of errors, and one list is full of errors, the other list was not full of errors, then it would -- then we'd have large inconsistencies between the lists. They are not large inconsistencies. There are some additional names on each of the lists but only a few hundred. So they really support each other, and we can now quite safely assume that these are lists based on the same population, the same sample of population that these people who went missing or were dead after the fall of -- of Srebrenica. And the information in those lists have been collected in quite different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mention "quite safely assume." Is that the right word, "assume"? We don't want people to assume or presume anything.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, no. We are close to concluding that these lists are based on the same populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we see here from this simple group of numbers for 2009 there's a -- it says 66.7 per cent. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That means -- that means 66.7 per cent or two-thirds exactly of the lists of missing persons have been identified as dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So there's a two-thirds overlap between your list and DNA-identified dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that one-third left over? Is that a -- is that a problem? Do we flunk the test or do we pass the test? What do you make of that last one-third?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If you look at that table, sir, you will see that in 2000 the per cent identified was .9 per cent or less than 1 per cent. Then it increased to approximately one-third in 2005, little more than half in 2008 and 2002 two-thirds in 2009. It's going up all the time, so that means that the number -- the proportion of missing persons who have not been found to be dead is going down all the time. We will never -- I don't think we will never find all the missing persons. They will not be -- identified all of them, but we'll -- we are getting closer and closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your work stopped in 2009?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The most -- yes. This testimony is based on the 2009 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you will hear updated reports from two witness, Ewa Tabeau and Dusan Janc on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this leftover 30-some odd per cent, is that a high error factor and how do you explain that 30-something odd per cent that doesn't fit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- perhaps I may have misunderstood the witness. It is not a matter of not fitting, but it is a matter of a limited number of bodies which were tested on DNA were found and were tested on DNA. Then it turned out that, in large numbers, it was able, we heard that evidence, to match those persons to family members which had given -- The simple -- without entering into your field of expertise but it's my understanding that if the remaining 30 per cent is not a group with very special features which would result in suddenly changing the outcome of the DNA test in a totally different way on any body found on from now, that it is a progressing confirmation of the assumptions that were made, and it's not a matter of passing the test yes or no. Future will tell us, but it becomes more and more unlikely that the results of the DNA tests of bodies not yet found would considerably differ from the outcome until now. That's my understanding of your testimony and I have great difficulties in understanding the questions put my Mr. McCloskey. Could you either decide in favour of Mr. McCloskey or in favour of my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to say that your comment on this was absolutely correct. I'm very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you refrain from any -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. McCloskey is hereby invited to put his next question to the witness .

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I was putting on my Mr. Ivetic hat to test of witness, of course, but thank you for that clarification. In fact, that might be a good time... all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I add one thing as to your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was just reflecting what I understood to be your testimony, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, I -- as time goes on, more and more bodies are found, and more and more are identified, DNA analysis is carried out, but it's now becoming increasingly difficult because the remaining bodies are more difficult to identify because one reason is that they found in many different graves. And if you found human remains in two or three or four different graves, it's a big puzzle to collect and to identify different human remains, different bones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard evidence about that and that -- when body parts are spread over all of the place then it causes additional problems. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will just -- and I know in your reports is -- that there have been challenges to your conclusions based on various documents and materials over the many years that you have been testifying, and I think that is addressed in your reports, and we -- perhaps we will hear from the Defence on some of those issues so I won't go -- I won't go into that. Except was there -- were there allegations that people that had -- were alive and well because they were on the voters list and should not, therefore, have been on the missing list, is that something -- I think you talked about that briefly before, but was that an allegation that was made that you looked into?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. But we -- we had already looked at that. And all those who were found on the voters list, those missing on the voters list, no one has been seen alive. They come up in statistical or analysis but they have not been seen. So that allegation is -- has been refuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then one last table I'd like to go to, 65 ter 25878, which was taken from your report as had this last one that we saw, so I won't be offering them into evidence at this point. If we could ... I think we really need to blow this up in one language or another. It's -- it's -- and we can call it: The distribution of Srebrenica-related missing and dead. All missing versus confirmed dead in percent. Now, I have to admit, I have never fully understood this graph. Can you tell us what this illustrates for your study?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. That top panel shows percentage distribution of all Srebrenica related missing and dead persons. That is those who are on the OTP 2009 missing list. It shows that the -- little more than 14 per cent of persons in age group 20 to 24 -- sorry, of all -- of all the missing, 14 per cent are in the age group 20 to 24. And 1 per cent are aged 70 to 74, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this based on the missing list information gained from relatives from your list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah. Remember that we have the year of birth for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So we -- and I know your report spells out the actual numbers of some of these age range from 10 years old to 19. I won't go into that. All right. So we understand that. That's from your list. What's the next one below that, if we could put that up. And it says: Identified and closed dead, with the same -- we have percentages and -- and lists again. What -- now we have things blacked out. What does that mean in relation to anything?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is the percentage distribution of those who have been found to be dead. And the absolute number is much smaller. It's about two-thirds of the top panel as we just heard. But the percentage distribution is remarkably similar. If we move one down, to the third panel, both -- we can see only the third panel is enough. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to interrupt. If we could put the third panel up by itself. So this is the first panel and the second panel listed next to each other basically?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we have missing lists and next to it we have the dead list. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, and it shows that the age distribution of those two groups of people are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It shows that the -- they come from the same population. There's nothing -- the dead persons are -- come from the same population as the missing persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you a question there. If we would have a different picture, for example, no one found above 60 which would then give a different picture, would that allow for the conclusion that they are not from the same population, or is it just a matter of the persons which were established to be dead, to -- would -- if they come from the same population as the persons missing, that it would be a representative portion of it rather than we only found the young ones, or we only found the old ones, or that it is -- in terms of age, representing a similar buildup of the population, a composition of the population, as the population from where these persons were reported missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to make this more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the -- the identified dead come from the same population as the missing -- I mean, they come from the missing population. Sorry, I was a bit unclear. That's what it shows. That they -- the dead come from the population on missing. They -- the missing come from sort of general population of all of Eastern Bosnia, but once they have been declared missing and there have been exhumations and identification, the age distribution of the dead is almost identical to the distribution of the missing with some differences. Perhaps that could clarify. We see that for the -- the youngest age groups, 15, 19 and 20 to 24, there are relatively more reported missing than had been identified as dead. And the reason for that could be that among the young men more walked through the forests and died on the way and were not found, therefore, not found in mass graves. So then a proportionally lower proportion of them have -- a relatively lower proportion of them have been identified as dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you one question. When said they come from the same population, you mean the population of persons having been reported as missing? That is what you call the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit confused about that, how you identified the population here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry for being unclear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for me, bad understanding. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. If the identified and closed are part of the -- come from the population that has been reported as missing, I -- I find it a little difficult to understand this graph where we now have, in -- if you look at, for instance, age 30 to 34, you have more dead than you have population. I would expect the black graph to be always be a -- a portion of the white graph, not ever to be greater. Am I right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Percentage in percentages can sometimes be difficult to handle and they're always straightforward. Because remember that the bars add to 100 per cent. The white bars and the dark, black bars add up to 100 per cent. When you look at 30 to 34, it means that approximately 11 per cent of the total number of missing persons are in that age group. But approximately 11.5 per cent of all those found to be dead are in that age groups. Is that -- but the absolute number of the black bar is, of course, much smaller -- is smaller than or less than the number of missing persons. You are right that the number of dead cannot exceed the missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now you said I was wrong, now you say I'm right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're right about absolute numbers, but you were not right about the percentage numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does this -- is this -- does this support the credibility of and accuracy of your missing list, the fact that these percentages are so close?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. It shows, for example, that the missing list was not made up by -- by somebody, by reporting fictitious persons or persons who were alive but not went missing, et cetera. So they -- they strongly support each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if there were large, relatively large numbers of false reports or people living in Greece, Slovenia, Portugal, would that be reflected in this graph?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Because then -- then -- if they belonged to a certain age group and not spread all over, then that would make the bars more different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As I said that -- this is always been a -- a tricky issue. But I thank you for your -- for your testimony. I do not have any other questions and we will wait until after the cross to offer anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Brunborg?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope to be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. I'd like to start off by looking at 65 ter number 11269 with you. And that will be your 2009 report and I'd like to turn to page 6 in both the English and the B/C/S. And that should bring us to the table that we were just looking at a few moments ago. Now, you, I think, identified that the number of persons identified by DNA is actually -- I wrote down 5.061, but in any event whether it's 5.061 or 5.053, for those people you cannot give us an opinion as to the exact details of where, when, and how they died to a degree of scientific certainty, can you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I was not tasked to do that. But in the -- in the appended list that was referred to, it is included the grave where they were found. So that says something about where they were found, not how they were died or where they died actually. You are right on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, we've seen both your 2007 curriculum vitae and we've seen the update, and I think I'm correct, and please tell me if that is so, that apart from the several cases that you have testified at this Tribunal as an expert witness, you have not testified as an expert witness at any trial in any other jurisdiction before any other court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, also looking at your CV, it appears that your degree is specialised in the field of economic demography; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of that field, would that be where you're trying to figure out incomes, how labour, how the labour force works, migration of labour, those sorts of topics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's one of the topics. Although in my dissertation I looked for economic factors affecting fertility decisions about -- decisions about how many children and when people should have children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. That was recorded and I had missed that in my notes. Now, in your prior employment with Statistics Norway - that is, prior to doing the work at the ICTY - did any of your work involve doing demographic studies of war zones, that is populations that were subject to an ongoing war?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. But I had worked in some African countries with data situations that were not very different from the situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What percentage of your work at Statistics Norway did this type of work entail, what you describe as being not very different from data situations in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That -- the expression not very different was between a country like Botswana and Bosnia where they don't have population registers which we have in Norway. Now, Bosnia did not have population register but they were close to having one, and they had personal identification number, and this is also what we have in my country. So a lot of my work has been studying and analysing data coming from so-called administrative registers and merging data from different registers, so which was highly relevant for my work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are you in a position to tell us approximately - doesn't have to be precise - what percentage of your work prior to coming to the ICTY dealt with applying demographic principles to examine and draw conclusions from an area of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I -- I had never worked on armed conflicts before but the basic principles and -- are the same whether you do demographic work in a country of peace or conflict. Many of the principles are the same. The main difference is that the data more faulty and they concern different events.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say that you had never worked on armed conflicts previously can we also conclude that you have not previously, prior to coming to the ICTY, published any papers on the topic of demography as applied to areas of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. But there are also -- there were very few papers on that all together by researchers all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, sir. And, in fact, wasn't it a rather novel approach in the field of demography at the time that you started performing the work that you did for the ICTY, this concept of applying demographic scientific principles to armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I would think so, although some people had done related work. What was novel about my work was that it was entirety based on what we call micro data, that is data on individuals. They are in conflict situations. Few cases where you have data on individuals. One other well known example is the Second World War where the 6 million Jews that were exterminated were known on both parties because both parties kept lists of what was going on. But in many other conflicts there are -- there's a large lack of names an information about the individuals who were affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that since you came to the ICTY and since you authored the reports on Srebrenica, for instance, one of which we have seen, the 2009 report today, that this area of work that you had not done previously has now become a significant part of your participation in commissions, speaking engagements, and working sessions since you've left the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is true, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, what's, for the Chamber, the relevance of this information? What should we learn from this? That the witness not let asleep the knowledge and experience he gained or what's, for our decisions, the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, to establish that the application of demography in the manner of studying armed conflicts is not a -- it's a -- it is still an experimental part of that field of study. That it's not one that has many years of development. It's a recent development in the field of demographic studies in the manner that it was done for these reports. That is the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what are we supposed to do that? That it' relatively new was already clear, isn't it? That you were lecturing about it would have made any difference if the witness would not have lectured about it. Would it be any less experimental? Would it be any -- I mean, the same as whether he testifies for the first time in a court, we wondered what the relevance of that is. I mean, if you are an expert you may never be called in your whole life to be examined in a court on your expertise and others may do. What's the relevance for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, but I would be very surprised to hear that that is an improper question for an expert witness, how many times they have testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's improper. It may be irrelevant and I'm inviting you to tell us the relevance of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Goes to the reliability of the expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether you testify or not -- I testified once in my life as an expert. Does that make me any less an expert in the field on which I testified?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a factor that is to be considered by a Court examining the testimony of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We are considering the answers the witness gives. That's the relevant issue. And not whether he testified five or ten times or never before. Please proceed. It's about relevance. It's not about whether it's proper or inappropriate. It's relevance, Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the work that did you here at the Tribunal, sir, am I correct that you had some student assistants who were actually performing some of the work with you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, some of these students co-authored some of the reports and some of the subsequent papers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these students -- first of all, I think we should identify the number of these students that assisted you. Could you -- I know of, I think, two. Am I correct that it was approximately two individuals?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: There were four altogether when I was employed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to these four individuals, can you tell me if they had at the time that they were working with you, were they still students or had they obtained degrees in any scientific field?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: One had obtained a degree in -- in informatics, I think, while the other ones were students but later graduated. Two of them have -- had very excellent careers, academic careers after they finished their work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the work that they did here, am I correct that they operated with a great deal of autonomy from you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That -- that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the work they did, am I correct that you did a lot of so-called consistency checks, random checking?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. But not only random checking, systematic checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's what I'm trying to find out, sir. In relation to your oversight or checking of the work done by these students, were there any parts of their work that would not have been subjected to your scrutiny?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: As long as I didn't sit next to them, I could not control every single step. But these were very able people, and what I could do more was to check their -- their findings, their aggregate findings, not every single step. But they were working under my guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to focus on the time-period when you first came to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to do so, I would like to, first of all, turn to 1D1162 and turn to page 5 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 6966 of the Blagojevic trial, if I've done my math correctly. I believe we need the prior page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I wanted to be very precise in terms of the language I use for your tasking or mandate from the OTP, so I thought I'd revisit your own words at lines 5 through 13 and you are welcome to follow along with me as I read it into the record: "Q. Now, in your discussions with Jean-Rene Ruez and Peter McCloskey, did you receive guidance in relation to whether you should be more liberal or more conservative or whatever in relation to your projects and indeed the numbers you were discussing? "A. They told me to do very strict and to be very careful, very conservative. And they also told me that I should only include persons who were registered as missing after the 11th of July, 1995, and only persons whose place of missing was related to the fall of Srebrenica, that is near Srebrenica." Does this accurately depict your tasking, as it were, from the Office of the Prosecutor when you first came to do your work for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But we agree that we should also include a few people who went -- reported as missing before 11th of July and after 1st of July. That is, 41, approximately 41 persons, since they could have last -- they could have been seen before 11th of July but went missing or went dead after 11th of July. A small number. But we did not include anybody who was reported as missing before the 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now as part of your mandate and your task that you received from the Office of the Prosecutor, were you asked to pay attention to the status of persons so as to differentiate between those registered as soldiers and those that were not?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was any part of your tasking or mandate concerned with differentiating whether persons had gone missing as part of the column of Bosnian Muslim males that left Srebrenica and went through the woods to try and break through to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, I was not. But I would like do add, as to the first part of that question, attention to the status of persons being soldiers that we -- after I left, my colleagues acquired lists on -- from the Bosnian army who had gone -- been killed, and -- and this list was merged with the list of missing. And 70 per cent of those who are reported as missing were also listed by the army as having been killed. But the army did not list any place of disappearance or cause of -- or cause of death or place of death, whether it was in combat or not. They listed death -- date of death but that appeared to be -- the quality of that information appeared to be poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just a few more questions about the mandate before we proceed to other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at 1D1163, page 70 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of one of your previous answers. You said: "... 70 per cent of those who are reported as missing were also listed by the army as having been killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, as being dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there may have been some traffic accidents or other, but I'm not quite sure about the exact wording whether they were killed or dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not the research you did yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was done after I left on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I will not ask any further questions about it to you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can call up 1D1163, page 70, and that is it on the screen. And this is a different day from the Blagojevic trial. I'd like to revisit some questions and answers from lines 11 through 20 with you rather than repeating them: "Q. I understand that this is your conclusion, based on this precise information. It is not a fact that they were certainly killed. "A. That is true. But all available evidence indicates that the missing men were dead -- are now dead. "Q. Out of this number, you cannot say how many men were killed in fighting, how many in trying to break through toward Tuzla, how many from self-inflicted wounds or through other collateral damage; is this correct? "A. That's true. That was not part of my mandate, to look at the causes of date and the circumstances under which they died." Does this accurately give more information as to the mandate, that this was not part of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I'd like to add, though, that the findings from exhumations and ICMP data analysis shows that a large number was found on the surface and not in mass graves. And it's -- so that's an indication that several of the men who went through were also dead. Who went -- I mean, men who walked through the forest towards Tuzla died on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And those men would be included in your list and in your overall figure that you've given for persons who have -- are missing and presumed deceased following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, normally speaking, and that would be in relation to other demographic studies or tradition demographic studies, is it customary for a demographer when coming to a conclusion to report a potential margin of error and thus a confidence level of the results?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In some cases, in some times of research that's done, but that depends on the circumstances of the study and the availability of data that makes it possible to estimate confidence levels. That is not always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the work that you did preparing reports and making findings as to Srebrenica, were you instructed to determine and report a potential margin of error or confidence level for those results?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. And I don't think -- see how that should be done. What we could have done is to include some cases of missing and perhaps dead also, as uncertain. But we -- we dropped all cases where we were not very convinced about the status. So we had one either include or not include. But we could have given probabilities to -- to matches, for example. That is done also in studies such as -- as this. This is it -- methods have been developed for -- in historical demography, matching names and attaching probabilities to the matches. But we did not do that. Probabilities are difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to -- and now on your CV there's a large number of published works that have you in the field of demography. In relation to those published works, am I correct that most of them have as part of their conclusions also a reporting on the confidence levels or margin of error based upon probabilities?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That -- that is mostly applicable when you -- when you do analysis based on sample studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to more traditional demographic studies, is there a well-defined methodology to estimate the sampling variance of the proportions involved so as to arrive at a margin of error?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. When you -- if you draw a random sample from a population, they are well-established and simple formula to establish the sample variance or the uncertainty of an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now when your information comes from various sources, whether primary or secondary in nature, would you, as a demographer normally look at control features to determine the credibility or reliability of those sources, such as looking at balancing errors and whole person imputations?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Sorry, you have to explain to me what you mean by balancing errors. I know what imputations are. That is assigning numbers to persons that are not really observe [sic] for those persons but we did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's my understanding that using the principle of balancing errors is a method to determine the confidence level of a particular source, whether it's trustworthy, more trustworthy, less trustworthy, to determine where potential errors might arise in the information that is reported therein?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I still don't understand what you mean by that. Could it be that these balancing errors occur if you look at the changes in a population. Have you a population one year is a population in the previous year, plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrations, minus out migrations. If those -- those figures don't fit together there is an error in one of the components, but we did not do -- our methodology was not based on this kind of reasoning. It would have been very nice if you could have had the census before the conflict then you have number of victims and then you have the census after the conflict. Then, especially comparing the census before and after conflict could say something about the number of victims. This has been done in situations with much less imperfect data, less perfect data than in Bosnia, say, Cambodia, where they did not have lists of persons who went missing or dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid any confusion later. You said this has been done in situations with less perfect data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More imperfect data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. The transcript was not clear on it yet. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now spend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I do, I think I should announce a break rather than invite you to continue. We'll take a break and -- after you have been escorted out of the courtroom, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Possible to get an estimate from Mr. Ivetic, just -- it may be planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may -- you're excused for the time being, Mr. Brunborg, until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe I have approximately one hour and 35, 40 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means there is a fair chance that you conclude your cross-examination well, let's say in it the first session or a little bit more tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I anticipate to, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break and resume at five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I take the opportunity as a follow-up from the housekeeping session this morning. First, in relation to D193, which was admitted but the Registrar is hereby instructed to replace the current English translation with the revised version, which was uploaded as 1D05-1741. A similar instruction will follow at the end of this session for D261 and D318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, would you agree with me that in that situation where you have an armed conflict that the parties to a conflict as well as organisations might have their own agenda or bias in terms of establishing figures, whether someone may want to play down figures whereas another party may want to play up figures. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's so vague. Organisations, parties, where is that going to take us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I say it that groups, persons with different interests may take a different approach in providing accurate numbers. Is that, Mr. Ivetic -- I'm wondering whether we are in the realm of an opinion about something which seems to be pretty obvious. I deny the objection. But, at the same time, Dr. Brunborg, would you agree that in -- what Mr. Ivetic told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. But I think that is the reason I was hired to work on the numbers and the number of missing and dead and other numbers in the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the work that you did, did you take any steps to determine what any potential biases or agendas the groups on whose lists you relied upon might have?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. We searched all the time for biases and wrong information. Being on the conservative side, as I said, we were looking for survivors among the missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to coming to the Tribunal, did you have occasion as part of your work in the field of Statistics Norway to study or become familiar with the census system or the population recording regime in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in general and Bosnia and Herzegovina in particular?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I had no previous experience with the censuses in the Balkans. But I had worked and was familiar with censuses in many other countries, including, Norway, United States, Botswana, Zambia and Palestine. And in the former Yugoslavia, censuses were carried out according to the international standards as printed, for example, in handbooks from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about the Yugoslav system as it pertained to identification registers, registers of births, registers of deaths?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's what we call vital statistics, which were also carried out, more or less, to international standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to revisit -- well, first of all, did you consult with any reference works, treatises, or publications written by others about the Yugoslav system to verify the method in which the vital statistics and the censuses were conducted?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I consulted a number of publications and institutions visiting, for example, the federal institute of statistics in Sarajevo. I also -- talking to the directors of the statistical institute for all of Bosnia with the three directors from the three major ethnic groups and reading many other articles, government notes, both from Belgrade regarding the system for all of Yugoslavia, and notes and reports replying to -- for Bosnia only.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to asking -- is it correct you also asked around of the various international organisations in pretty much anyone you could think of to try and figure out what organisations had been keeping figures, where those figures might be, and what form they might be. And when I say international organisations, the Office of the High Representative, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, I met with all of those in Sarajevo and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you started, and I think it's still true today, you did not have a reliable and a definite base-line of how many people were residing in Srebrenica just prior to 11 July 1995. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's true. Reports indicated 40.000 at the most, 5.000 less at the least, but these were not considered reliable since we did not have any lists of the number of people they included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct, sir, that these figures that were estimates were, in part, based on reporting that had been done to humanitarian organisations for the obtaining of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is my understanding, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also your opinion that this figure may be somewhat inflated because persons wanted to get more rations or more aid and so they over-reported the numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness said that they were not considered reliable. Is -- is -- do you want to know why they were not reliable if -- for this witness? Because you're now asking about what possibly could make them unreliable. Where the witness said, We considered them unreliable for his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the two lists which were the primary source of your work, the PHR and the ICRC lists, am I correct that these lists themselves were not complete in terms of the data they contained, and for one example did not both have the unique identifier, the JMBG, or in B/C/S, "Maticni Broj" for everyone?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: These two lists did not include the "Maticni Broj" for anybody, as far as I remember, but the census did. The voters list did not include -- yeah, sorry. The voters list included that number for large number of people, and the census for large number of people, but there were also significant number who did not have that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can take a look at 65 ter number 04510 and page 4 of the same in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this will be your 12 February 2000 report. That will be coming up. And in the middle of the page, in the English, the second paragraph before the methodology section, it reads as follows sir: "In both lists there are many empty fields. In the ICRC list the least frequently completed items are date of birth (65.4 per cent complete) and date of disappearance (89.6 per cent). The year of these events is included for almost everybody, however. For the PHR list the least complete items are date of birth (78.2 per cent) and the place of disappearance (80.7 per cent). The other variables are recorded for almost everybody, but that does not necessarily mean they're always correct. Errors are particularly common in the spelling of names of persons and places." And I'd like to stop there and ask you, sir, are these observations contained in your earlier report accurately and truthfully depicting the state of the ICRC and PHR lists?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Absolutely. Although the percentages may have changed somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the section labelled methodology, it's on the same page in English. It's on the next page in B/C/S. You talk about the unique ID number. And you state as follows: "Although a unique ID number was introduced in Yugoslavia in 1981, it is not used by ICRC and PHR in their databases. Moreover when it is used, such as in the 1991 census and the OSCE voters' register, it is sometimes missing or wrong." Does that -- I'd like to ask if you could explain for us when you say that the JMB -- pardon me, the unique ID number is sometimes missing or wrong, what is that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In the census in 1991 enumerators went around to households and are interviewed usually the head of the household and asked for name, full name, father's name, everybody in the household, date of birth, the "Maticni" -- the full "Maticni Broj," JMBG. And in -- for some of the people they either did not know it or say if the man was absent in the household and their wife was there, she did not know her husband's "Maticni Broj." Could be so -- so then it was just not entered. It was not widely known by -- it was not known that number by everybody as it is in the Scandinavian countries today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I understand that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I understand correct, you have something that you need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it would be -- that takes only one minute, but if this would be a suitable moment for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To stop for the day. Mr. Brunborg, we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.30, and -- but before you leave, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow, and we expect that it certainly will not take the whole of the morning to complete your testimony. At least that's what we hope. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I'm aware of the restrictions on my behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, I'd like to make -- to give two similar instructions to the Registry. This morning, D261 was admitted into evidence, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the initial document, which was 1D00845, with the revised version, which is uploaded as 1D00845A. Similar instruction for D318, also admitted. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registrar to replace the current document, which was known as 1D01068, with the revised version, which was uploaded as 1D01068A. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 26th of July, 2013, in this same courtroom, III, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 26th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.14 p.m.,
